newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus launches new, bigger A340 models.
newsitem.headline: Airbus launches new, bigger A340 models.

text.p: Airbus Industrie chief Jean Pierson announced Sunday that the European aircraft maker was launching two new versions of its A340 widebody jetliner, a move aimed at winning over customers of Boeing's popular 747.

The company was looking for customers to make commitments to help launch the long-range A340-500 and the larger-capacity 378-seat A340-600, the Airbus managing director said at a news conference at the Paris air show. Total investment would be $2.5 billion for the project, he said.
Given the costs involved, it was "mandatory to seek a launch customer for this programme," he said, adding he hoped to have an airline customer lined up by September.

The A340-600 will be ready for passenger service in the fall of 2001, Airbus said. It said that the plane, a stretched version of earlier A340 models, was "an attractive replacement for early model Boeing 747s" with lower operating costs and more range than the 747-400.

The new plane is a stop-gap measure aimed at attacking Boeing's dominance in the market for large jetliners with its 777 giant twinjet and the 747 jumbo jet, industry officials said. In the longer term, Airbus wants to launch a 500-seat aircraft to overtake the 747.

The A340-500 will be similar to the 600 model but with a shorter fuselage and more range. It will carry 313 passengers and will be able to fly non-stop from London to Perth, making it the world's longest range airliner, Airbus said.
The new jets will initially be powered by Rolls Royce Trent 500 engines, with thrust of around 56,000 pounds.
Pierson said the contract with Rolls-Royce was not exclusive, meaning a second engine supplier could be chosen. He did not elaborate.
Airbus had been looking at Pratt & Whitney PW4500 engines for the new planes, after failing to get price discounts from General Electric Aircraft Engines, officials said.
In a statement, Pierson said Airbus selected the Trent 500 because of its low noise, high fuel efficiency and low operating costs.
"It offers the market the best technical and commercial combination together with the greatest flexibility," he said.
Separately, Airbus' British partner said that if the four-nation consortium failed to resolve differences over its corporate structure it would scrap plans to build the world's first superjumbo jet.

The head of British Aerospaces said that Airbus' planned A3XX project would not be viable without the efficiencies that a company restructuring would bring. Airbus wants to make the A3XX for airlines to use in 2003. But development costs are estimated at at least $8 billion.
